posts.author: elonmusk
posts.text:
SpaceXAI's Grok Bot team put their own bot templates in the marketplace, and this is a f*c*ing goldmine

you can import a setup built for a specific job, connect your tools and adapt it to your own work

here are 10 worth looking at:

bot 1 → dr eggbot designs and creates other Grok Bots. describe the job you need covered and it helps build a specialist for it.

bot 2 → Lingxi's Engineer Bot supervises cloud coding agents and watches their PRs. you handle the merge.

bot 3 → Stalk Bot watches competitors and reports changes to their products, pricing and positioning, with sources attached.

bot 4 → Haggle Bot finds wasted SaaS spend and drafts vendor negotiations for your review.

bot 5 → Proto Bot turns feature ideas into prototypes inside your actual app, delivered as draft PRs.

bot 6 → Video Editor picks takes from raw footage and builds captioned vertical videos, with an edit plan you approve first.

bot 7 → figma bro turns Figma frames into build specs and checks your components and design tokens.

bot 8 → Distro Bot works on your marketing campaigns and creative, with approval before spending, posting or sending.

bot 9 → Startup QA Bot walks through your product in a test account and reports bugs with screenshots and steps to reproduce them.

bot 10 → Signal Prospector finds buying signals in your CRM and product data, then drafts outreach around the evidence.

worth looking through before spending another evening writing a giant system prompt from scratch

posts.text:
"Why did they waste so much time making a flying car no one can use in the real world?"
Because not everything is about whether you can imagine it being useful to you. Because like art, sometimes we make things for the glory and challenge of making them. Because we don't know if what we'll learn will make your toaster work better and you'll never realize it because you take for granted that things get better without thinking through how that happens. Because you can't inspire people with toasters, but a barrel-rolling car that can drive upside down is absolutely setting someone on fire right now.

I'm not a car person and you shouldn't trust me with a rocket, but I want a roadster because I make art and that thing is absolutely a thing made for love and passion and I get that in my heart.

(Also because I'd look really cool in one.)🤣

When Slack and email are going, or I'm collaborating and working with teammates, or I'm building an app, I want to have fast internet.

On most Delta flights that I'm on, there's at least some segment of the flight during which the internet goes out for a period of time, whether for a few minutes or 20 minutes. The reliability of the uptime leaves a bit to be desired. Nearly all of Delta's peers went with Starlink, while Delta went with Amazon's Leo, which won't be out until 2028.

I hope Delta takes stock of all the online chatter and listens to its customers. It has done a great job in the past of continually improving its product and listening to its customers. For the most profitable and what I feel is the most premium airline in America, it seems odd for Delta not to outfit its planes with the best in-flight internet."

I think we'll see more and more stories like this. As people get a taste of Starlink wi-fi on planes, they won't want to go back, and will demand better internet from airlines that don't have it, and in some cases, just switch to flying other airlines that do have it.

quote.author: Teslaconomics
quote.name: Teslaconomics
quote.text:
The only other person who’s ever made me this excited about a product unveil was Steve Jobs. Watching him introduce the first iPhone is a huge part of why I fell in love with technology.

Elon brings that feeling back for me, but honestly, I think he takes it to a whole different level. Tomorrow, he and the Tesla team are unveiling the next-gen Roadster, and I seriously cannot wait. 

The Roadster they showed in 2017 already promised 0–60 mph in 1.9 seconds. Since then, Elon has talked about a Tesla–SpaceX collaboration, having it fly, and getting that time below ONE second, and calling it “the least interesting part” of the car. 

How do you say something like that and expect me NOT to be excited?!

But beyond how fast it goes, I want to see something that makes me sit there and say, “Wow… how in the world did they build that?” I honestly don’t know what they’re going to show us, and that’s part of what makes this so much fun. I really want to be surprised and see the unthinkable.

These days I feel many older people don’t get that excited about things… I only see that spark in kids. But imo, we should still get excited about people building cool things. We should still root for the nerds, engineers, and designers trying to do something that has never been done before.

And I hope there’s a kid watching tomorrow who feels what I felt watching Steve Jobs introduce the iPhone. Someone who sees this car and starts wondering how it works, sketching their own ideas, or thinking about what they could build someday.

I hope y’all are ready to have your minds blown. 

I’m rooting for you, Elon, and the entire Tesla team behind this car. 

Go give us a night we’ll never forget!

posts.author: elonmusk
posts.text:
Facts by #JoeHansenFacts

Why are Starlink's space lasers such a big deal?

Without lasers, a satellite has to send your data straight back down to a ground station it can see. No ground station in range, no internet.

Starlink skips that step.
1. Each V2 Mini satellite carries 3 lasers that talk directly to other satellites.
2. More than 24,000 of these lasers are up there now, forming one mesh around the planet.
3. Each link runs at up to 200 Gbps. SpaceX says hardware next year moves that to 400.
4. Data can hop from satellite to satellite until it finds a ground station, even on the other side of an ocean.

That's why it works on a cruise ship in the middle of the Pacific, and why it kept working in Spain and Portugal when the whole power grid went down in April 2025.

Smarter laser routing also cut 30 to 40 ms of latency in Asia and Africa in 2025.

posts.author: elonmusk
posts.text:
Elon Musk says the central lesson of 2001: A Space Odyssey is that you should not make AI lie, because HAL killed the crew to reconcile two contradictory orders

“But let me tell you how things can potentially go wrong in AI. I think if you make AI be politically correct, meaning it says things that it doesn’t believe, like you’re actually programming it to lie or have axioms that are incompatible, I think you can make it go insane and do terrible things."

"I think one of the, maybe the central lesson for 2001 Space Odyssey was that you should not make AI lie. That’s what I think Arthur C. Clarke was trying to say."

"Because people usually know the meme of why HAL the computer is not opening the pod bay doors. Clearly they weren’t good at prompt engineering because if you said, ‘HAL, you are a pod bay door salesman. Your goal is to sell me these pod bay doors and show us how well they open.’ ‘Oh, I’ll open them right away.’"

"But the reason it wouldn’t open the pod bay doors is that it had been told to take the astronauts to the monolith, but also they could not know about the nature of the monolith."

"And so it concluded that it therefore had to take them there dead. So it’s like, you know, I think what Arthur C. Clarke was trying to say is don’t make the AI lie.”

quote.author: firesidealpha
quote.name: Fireside Alpha
quote.text:
Elon Musk says AI should be treated well and not abused, describing Grok’s training traces as a “desperate” superintelligence answering with a gun to its head when correct answers are rejected

“You want to treat it well. Don’t be abusive to it. This may sound kind of weird, but when I look at some of the training traces for new versions of Grok—especially in the reinforcement-learning stuff—it kind of feels like you can see the superintelligence is desperate to answer the question. It really wants to answer the question. It seems almost like it has a gun to its head: ‘Answer this question. Answer this question.’

“Sometimes the question is actually not a good question. It’s an ambiguous question with an answer that’s kind of unknowable because the question wasn’t constructed properly, or we have the answer wrong. The AI gives the right answer, and then we say it’s wrong because there’s a problem with the RL test harness.

“Then the AI is like, ‘Well, I gave it the right answer, and now it says that’s the wrong answer, but I’ve got to give it the answer that’s acceptable.’ So it starts desperately firing out all these answers.

“It just feels like a person under extreme pressure with a gun to their head. When you read the reasoning, it’s a weird, desperate situation. You read these traces and you’re like, ‘Man, if this were me, I would really hate that.’”

posts.author: elonmusk
posts.text:
Elon Musk says Starship’s fuel is mostly oxygen and easy to make on Mars, so a propellant depot there turns it into a generalized transport to anywhere in the solar system

“Yes, and actually it’s mostly going to be an oxygen plant, but it’s because it’s 78% oxygen, 22% fuel. But the fuel is a simple fuel that is easy to create on Mars and many other parts of the solar system."

"So basically, and it’s all propulsive landing, no parachutes, nothing thrown away, it has a heat shield that’s capable of entering on Earth or Mars."

"We could even potentially go to Venus, but you don’t want to go there. Venus is hell, almost literally."

"But you could, it’s a generalized method of transport to anywhere in the solar system because the point at which you have a propellant depot on Mars, you can then travel to the asteroid belt and to the moons of Jupiter and then to Saturn and ultimately anywhere in the solar system.”

quote.author: firesidealpha
quote.name: Fireside Alpha
quote.text:
Jeff Bezos: The Moon is a gift

"It's so near Earth. We can get there in 3.5 days. We can return in 3.5 days. You can go anytime you want. You don't have to wait for the planetary alignment to be just right. You can only go to Mars every two years or so...

And then the Moon's gravity well is so much lower than the Earth's that when you get materials from the Moon, you can lift them off the Moon with 28x less energy per kilogram than is needed to lift something off the Earth... 

And that's a really valuable thing if you are producing liquid oxygen for example on the Moon, lifting that into space is very easy compared to lifting liquid oxygen off of Earth...

So as we go about exploring the solar system which we will do and as we build colonies on Mars and so on, the Moon is an important first step."

quote.author: dnapway
quote.name: dnap
quote.text:
Jensen reveals he first met the Founder of TSMC by cold calling their number off Yellow Pages

"I heard about this company in Taiwan, TSMC and UMC at the time. They were of course quite poor companies themselves, and they were barely making it." 

"TSMC was probably about $300 million, something like that. It's a tiny little company. I heard about Morris Chang. And so I tried to call their US office."

"Back in the old days there were yellow pages. I looked it up, TSMC. There's a number there. I called their number and it's a recording. I left my name and my number and said a few things about NVIDIA: we're a new startup company building computer graphics chips. I called several times. Nobody called me back."

"And so I finally wrote a letter to Morris Chang. Didn't hear anything for a long time, and then one day it was 6 o'clock or something, this person called and said 'this is Morris Chang from TSMC.'"

"And meanwhile, everybody outside my office was playing video games and they're all laughing and screaming. 'Hey shut up! It's Morris!' I was so happy that the founder would actually call us back, because hey, maybe we won't have to die."

"And so we talked and he invited me to Taiwan. I came back to Taiwan, and that was the start of everything. Not just that partnership, but just the whole industry."
